28  certain claims were adjudicated via JMOL, suggesting it was appropriate for the fact 
1  finder to hear the expert testimony even if it ultimately proved unpersuasive.   
2       “The motivation to combine prior art references can come from the knowledge of 
3  those skilled in the art, from the prior art reference itself, or from the nature of the 
4  problem to be solved.”  Acoustic Tech., Inc. v. Itron Networked Sols., Inc.,
949 F.3d 5
  1366, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2020).  On its face, Dr. Turk’s report meets these criteria.  His 
6  report contains analysis Park Assist can test or contest about the motivation a person of 
7  ordinary skill in the art would have to combine prior art references.  Park Assist can 
8  challenge Dr. Turk using cross-examination or its own evidence, as other courts have 
9  found when addressing factual issues on motivating prior artwork.  See, e.g., Cellular 
10  Communs. Equip., LLC v. Apple Inc., No. 6:14-cv-251,
2016 WL 6884076
, at *3 (E.D. 
11  Tex. Aug. 30, 2016); Equistar Chemicals, LP v. Westlake Chem. Corp., 6:14CV68, 2016
12 WL 4410050
, at *3 (E.D. Tex. Feb. 26, 2016).                              
13            ii.  Evidence Showing How References Can Be Combined            
14       Beyond analysis requiring evidence of motivation to combine, obviousness also 
15  requires some teaching of how the references could be combined to work together.  See, 
16  Power-One, Inc. v. Artesyn Techs., Inc.,
599 F.3d 1343, 1351
 (Fed. Cir. 2010).  Here, 
17  Park Assist asserts Dr. Turk simply cherry picks elements from various references, gives 
18  no second thought about technical problems or challenges that may arise, and is not clear 
19  as to how his proposed combinations would work.  ECF No. 138, at 9-10.  This Court 
20  disagrees.                                                                
21       Dr. Turk’s report provides detailed analysis that could assist a jury in determining 
22  the question of invalidity of the ‘956 Patent for obviousness.  As this Court stated in 
23  Section III(a)(i), supra, Dr. Turk’s report references primary and secondary sources in 
24  analyzing the obviousness issues and demonstrates how a person of ordinary skill in the 
25  art could use the references to combine them and improve existing ideas.  Moreover, the 
26  combined references are all in the field of camera-based parking management systems.  
27  From their pleadings, it appears Park Assist’s disagreements are with the conclusions 
28  drawn by Dr. Turk and his methodology in reaching said conclusions.  This goes towards 
1  the weight, not the admissibility, of Dr. Turk’s testimony and, as previously stated, can 
2  be addressed during cross-examination or with other evidence.             
3            iii.  Alleged Improper Combination of References                
4       One of the selections of artwork Dr. Turk analyzed in his obviousness analysis is 
5  the “M3 Product.”  Regarding the M3 Product, the parties disagree on how the product 
6  has evolved and whether Dr. Turk should have addressed the evolution.  Park Assist 
7  claims, “Dr. Turk treats multiple different references related to the M3 Product as a single 
8  article – drawing his analysis from whichever reference he believes best shows a given 
9  claim element . . . Dr. Turk is thus using his single “M3” reference [as] a mishmash of 
10  different references, without any word of why this is proper and without discussing any 
11  motivation to combine these multiple M3 references.”  ECF No. 138, at 14.  Indect 
12  argues,                                                                   
13       “Park Assist cannot claim that all of the documents that constitute the M3, as 
14       set forth in Dr. Turk’s report are about a different product – they all disclose 
15       feature of the M3 sold by Park Assist before the priority date of the ‘956 
16       patent.  As such, there is nothing to combine, the documents are neither 
17       describing different products offered by Park Assist, nor describing products 
18       from Park Assist and another source.”                                
19  ECF No. 164, at 20.  The parties’ pleadings yet again indicate a reasonable disagreement 
20  on Dr. Turk’s methodology and the conclusions he reaches which are subjects 
21  appropriate for cross examination.  Park Assist fails to persuade this Court that exclusion 
22  is necessary under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 or Daubert.               
23       Park Assist claims Indect is attempting to persuade this Court to forego its 
24  responsibilities under Daubert and “leave it to Park Assist to address the baseless Turk 
25  opinion with cross examination.”  ECF No. 138, at 8.  In support of this claim, Park 
26  Assist cites Innogenetics, N.V. v. Abbott Laboratories,
512 F.3d 1363
 (Fed. Cir. 2008) 
27  and Deckers Outdoor Corp. v. Romeo & Juliette, Inc.,
2017 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 217136
, 
28  *9-10 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 6, 2017).  In Innogenetics, the Federal Circuit found the district 
1  court did not abuse its discretion in precluding expert testimony on obviousness when the 
2  expert “merely list[ed] a number of prior art references and then conclude[d] with the 
3  stock phrase ‘to one skilled in the art it would have been obvious to perform’ . . . .” 
4  Innogenetics at. 1373.  The court stated, “nowhere does [the expert] state how or why a 
5  person ordinarily skilled in the art would have found the claims of the [] patent obvious in 
6  light of some combination of those particular references.”
Id. at 1373
.  In Deckers, the 
7  expert proffered that it would have been obvious to modify the reference, but did not state 
8  why or provide any motivation.  Deckers at 9-10.                          
9       Having reviewed the Turk Report, this Court finds it offers far more than the 
10  conclusory statements described in Innogenetics and Deckers.  Dr. Turk’s report 
11  describes with specificity how the prior art references can be combined and identifies the 
12  limitations taught by each primary reference and secondary reference.  This goes well 
13  beyond conclusory statements and provides the factfinder evidence which may support 
14  Indect’s claims of obviousness.                                           
15            iv.  Scope of Testimony                                         
16       “The ultimate test of patent invalidity is one of law . . . but resolution of the 
17  obviousness issue necessarily entails several basic factual inquiries.”  Sakraida v. Ag Pro, 
18  Inc.,
425 U.S. 273, 280
 (1976).  To the extent that an expert purports to offer a legal 
19  opinion on an ultimate issue, such testimony must be excluded because “offering legal 
20  conclusion testimony invades the province of the trial judge.”  Nationwide v. Kass Info. 
21  Sys., Inc.,
523 F.3d 1051, 1059
 (9th Cir. 2008); Mukhtar, 299 F.3d at 1066 n.10 ("[A]n 
22  expert witness cannot give an opinion as to her legal conclusion, i.e., an opinion on an 
23  ultimate issue of law.").  While expert testimony can be used to provide evidence of the 
24  state of the art, how one of ordinary skill in the art would understand the prior art 
25  references, and whether one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to 
26  combine or modify prior art references in a manner that yields the claimed invention, it is 
27  improper to provide testimony that is merely a legal conclusion.          
28       Having reviewed the Turk Report, this Court concludes it passes muster under the 
1  reliability and relevance requirements of Daubert and Rule 702.  Therefore, Park Assist’s 
2  request to preclude Dr. Turk’s testimony entirely is denied.  Dr. Turk’s testimony, 
3  however, must not serve as a substitute for jury instructions on obviousness or make 
4  conclusory statements that the ‘956 patent should be invalidated on obviousness grounds. 
5       B. Motions to Seal                                                   
6       Concurrent with the parties’ briefing on the Turk Motion to Preclude, the parties 
7  move to file under seal portions of their briefs, declarations, and supporting exhibits.  The 
8  selections contain, reference, or discuss commercially sensitive and proprietary business 
9  data.  The documents have been previously designated “Confidential,” “Confidential – 
10  For Counsel Only,” or “Confidential – For Counsel Only – Prosecution Bar” pursuant to 
11  the Protective Order issued in this case.  See ECF No. 43.  Specifically, these selections 
12  ostensibly contain business information including trade secrets, confidential research, and 
13  other financial or commercial information.                                
14       “[C]ompelling reasons sufficient to outweigh the public’s interest in disclosure and 
15  justify sealing court records exist when such court files might . . . become a vehicle for 
16  improper purposes, such as the use of records to . . . release trade secrets.”  Kamakana v. 
17  City & Cnty. of Honolulu,
447 F.3d 1172
, 1179 (9th Cir. 2006).  A “trade secret may 
18  consist of any formula, pattern, device or compilation of information which is used in 
19  one’s business, and which gives him an opportunity to obtain an advantage over 
20  competitors who do not know or use it.”  The Court can seal proprietary information to 
21  protect a business from potential harm.  See Obesity Research Institute, LLC v. Fiber 
22  Research International, LLC, No. 15-CV-00595-BAS-MDD,
2017 WL 6270268
, at *2 
23  (S.D. Cal. Dec. 8, 2017) (granting motion to file documents containing proprietary 
24  business information under seal).
